strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored problem: generating compositional, interactive 3D scenes with correct object-object spatial relationships (OOR) rather than monolithic baked meshes. The 'generate-then-compose' reformulation of compositional generation as a structured 3D registration problem is a sensible and useful insight.

The pipeline is training-free and modular, combining image editing priors (Nano Banana Pro), 3D foundation models (TRELLIS2), part segmentation (PartField), and a well-motivated two-stage composition: global-to-local registration (OBB + GeoTransformer + scale-aware ICP) for the anchor, followed by a differentiable SDF-based collision loss with a schedule that smoothly transitions from pure alignment to physics-aware refinement (Eq. 2-3).

The VLM-based agentic refinement loop that detects persistent collisions in multi-view renderings (including cross-sections), generates corrective editing prompts, and re-integrates revised geometry is an interesting mechanism for fixing geometric mismatches that rigid transformations cannot resolve, and it is illustrated in detail (Figs. 4, 9).

The released compositional dataset (~8,300 scenes, ~7,700 two-object and ~600 multi-object) is a substantial contribution relative to prior pairwise composition datasets (e.g., 2BY2's 517 pairs), with per-scene assets and compositional poses, and it is stated to be publicly released.

Qualitative evidence is extensive: multi-baseline comparisons (Fig. 6, 10), multi-part compositions (Figs. 5, 11, 12), multi-view renderings to expose hidden flaws (Figs. 13-15), and honest failure-case analysis (Fig. 8, A.3). The limitations discussion (fine-grained/tightly-coupled components, 2D occlusion ambiguity) is candid and meaningful.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a serious concern. The core of the pipeline depends on closed, proprietary systems: Nano Banana Pro / Gemini 3 Pro for image generation, editing, and VLM analysis, plus TRELLIS2 and a commercial Rodin/Hunyuan3D website. The exact prompts are given but model behavior may change or be inaccessible; the code release URL is incomplete ('will be released on'). This limits independent verification of the claims.

The quantitative evaluation is thin: only 10 test cases, with CLIP-based semantic metrics (a weak proxy for 3D compositional fidelity) and intersection ratios. No statistics, variance, or larger-scale evaluation is provided despite the authors having an 8,300-scene dataset at their disposal; the small test set also risks selection bias.

Baseline fairness is questionable. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are learned methods trained on different data distributions and receive no text/image conditioning, so their poor generalization is expected rather than a meaningful comparison; 2BY2 was retrained from scratch by the authors without disclosed details. A more informative comparison would be against zero-shot or VLM-guided composition baselines such as COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE, which the paper cites but does not compare against.

The claimed 'physically-sound' property is only measured as mesh interpenetration (surface/volume intersection ratios). No simulation-based validation (e.g., gravity settling, contact/support checks in a physics engine) is performed, so stability of compositions (objects resting on stands, shoes inside cabinets) is not actually verified, despite the robot-simulation motivation in the introduction.

Technical novelty is limited: the individual components (GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, OBB scale initialization, ReLU-clipped SDF penalties) are established techniques, and the contribution is primarily a systems/engineering integration plus a dataset. For an Algorithms/General contribution, deeper ablations (e.g., contribution of the beta schedule, soft repulsion term, agentic loop success rates, cost/iterations) are expected but largely absent; the agentic refinement is evaluated only qualitatively.

Dataset quality and provenance are under-specified: no description of filtering/validation of the 8,300 scenes, no reporting of failure rates across the automatic pipeline, and unclear licensing/attribution of underlying 3D assets.

Presentation issues reduce polish: multiple typos ('collsion-aware', 'overlop', 'occulsion', 'Irenderd', 'muli-view'), malformed/incomplete reference entries, an incomplete code-release sentence, and equations carried over with raw LaTeX in the source.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem—compositional/interactive 3D asset generation with object-object spatial relationships—which is underserved relative to single-asset 3D generation.

The generate-then-compose reformulation is a sensible, clearly articulated idea: using a 2D-edited scene image reconstructed by a 3D foundation model purely as spatial guidance, rather than as the final asset, avoids the hole/artifact problems of direct part segmentation.

The two-stage composition (global-to-local registration for the anchor, SDF-based collision-aware optimization for the remaining object) is technically coherent and the collision losses in Eqs. 2-3 are reasonable and well motivated.

The closed-loop VLM-driven agentic refinement is an interesting mechanism for correcting fundamentally incompatible geometries that rigid/SDF transforms cannot fix, and it is illustrated with concrete failure-and-recovery examples (Figs. 4, 9).
The paper is honest about failure modes (symmetric objects, occlusion-propagated errors) and about the limitations of 2D spatial priors.
The released dataset of ~8,300 compositional scenes with compositional poses could be a useful community resource, being an order of magnitude larger than 2BY2's 517 pairs.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source, proprietary components (Nano Banana Pro for image editing/generation, Gemini 3 Pro as the VLM, Rodin/Hunyuan3D web tools). The entire pipeline's behavior is tied to unversioned commercial APIs whose outputs are not reproducible, and the paper cannot be reproduced without paid access to these services. This is a serious concern for a systems/pipeline paper.

The quantitative evaluation is very thin: only 10 test cases, split across two figures. Statistical significance is impossible to establish at this scale, and cherry-picking risk is high. There is no evaluation on a held-out set drawn from the authors' own 8,300-scene dataset, which would have been natural and cheap to run.

There are no ablation studies. The three proposed components (global-to-local registration, SDF collision loss, agentic refinement) are never quantitatively disentangled; the claimed benefits of the agentic loop in particular are supported only by two qualitative walkthroughs.

Baselines are weak or mismatched. Jigsaw is a fractured-object assembly method and 2BY2 is trained on a small daily-object dataset with no released weights (so the authors retrained it themselves, with unknown fidelity). COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE [7], the most directly related text-guided composition method discussed in Related Work, is not compared against. The 'PartField' baseline is not a composition method at all, so half of Table 2 is not applicable ('/').

The CLIP-based semantic metrics are partially circular: the Image CLIP metric compares the final rendering against the Nano Banana Pro-generated guidance image, i.e., against the very prior the pipeline is built on, so high scores partly measure fidelity to the guiding generator rather than composition quality.

The dataset contribution is under-specified: no description of how prompts/scenarios were sampled, no quality filtering or validation statistics, no annotation protocol, and no evidence that poses in the released dataset are physically correct beyond the same pipeline being evaluated. It is unclear whether the dataset is validated or merely generated and aggregated.

Novelty is limited at the component level: OBB initialization, GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, SDF penetration penalties, and VLM-in-the-loop editing are all established techniques; the contribution is their orchestration. This would be acceptable if the evaluation were convincing, but the evidence base (10 cases, no ablations) does not establish that the orchestration is robust.

Writing quality needs improvement: recurring typos ('collsion-aware', 'overlop, occulsion', 'muli-view', 'Copy-trasform-paste'), an incomplete sentence in the abstract ('The code will be released on'), and Eq. 2 contains a malformed expression with mismatched parentheses/angle brackets. These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The claimed downstream motivation (robot Sim2Real training) is not validated at all: no physical property annotation, no demonstration that the generated scenes are usable in a physics simulator, no contact/stacking stability checks. The robot-learning framing in the introduction is thus largely decorative.
Runtime/cost of the pipeline is never reported, despite it requiring multiple 4K image generations, two TRELLIS2 reconstructions, PartField segmentation, and up to 5 agentic iterations per scene.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically important problem: generating compositional, physically plausible interactive 3D scenes (with correct object-object spatial relationships) rather than monolithic fused assets, motivated well by the Sim2Real/robot-learning data bottleneck.

The generate-then-compose reformulation is a sensible and clearly motivated idea: using image-guided 3D generation (TRELLIS2) plus PartField segmentation purely as spatial guidance, while preserving high-fidelity individual meshes, sidesteps the hole/artifact problems of direct scene segmentation (Fig. 2).

The two-stage composition pipeline is technically reasonable: global-to-local registration (OBB scale alignment + GeoTransformer warm start + scale-aware ICP) followed by a differentiable SDF-based collision loss with a progressive schedule is well-formulated and addresses real failure modes of naive registration (orientation inversion, interpenetration).

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop is a novel and interesting mechanism for correcting fundamentally incompatible geometries that rigid-pose optimization cannot fix, with convincing case studies (Figs. 4, 9).
A large interactive composition dataset (~8,300 scenes with poses) is promised, significantly larger than 2BY2's 517 pairs, which would be a valuable community resource.

Honest limitations discussion: failure cases (symmetric objects causing inversion, occlusion-induced error propagation) and future-work discussion of 2D-prior limitations are substantive rather than token.
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source, proprietary components (Nano Banana Pro for image generation/editing, Gemini 3 Pro as VLM, Rodin/Hunyuan3D websites) undermines reproducibility; the pipeline may be impossible to replicate exactly even with released code, and results may shift silently as commercial models are updated.

Quantitative evaluation is very thin: only 10 test cases (5 in Fig. 6 + 5 in Fig. 7), and CLIP-based semantic metrics are weak proxies for compositional correctness. There are no ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual components (e.g., agentic optimization vs. SDF stage alone, λ, βmax, kmax, iteration limits), despite a multi-component pipeline.

Novelty is primarily in system integration: the individual ingredients (scale-aware ICP, Umeyama, GeoTransformer, SDF penalty terms, VLM-in-the-loop correction) are established; the collision loss in Eq. (2)-(3) is a fairly standard penetration penalty. The scientific depth is limited for an Algorithms/General contribution.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or complete: Jigsaw and 2BY2 are trained for different tasks (fracture assembly, 517-pair dataset) and do not optimize scale; the most directly relevant training-free competitor, COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE, is cited but not compared against.

The dataset's quality is not validated: since scenes are produced by the same automated (potentially error-prone) pipeline, the paper does not describe filtering, human verification, or error rates in the 8,300 scenes, which matters greatly for its utility as a benchmark or training resource.

Presentation issues: repeated typos ('collsion-aware', 'overlop, occulsion', 'Irenderd'), a nearly empty code-release sentence ('The code will be released on'), and reliance on future-dated references (2026) for core tools suggest the manuscript needed another proofreading pass.

The claim of 'physically-sound' scenes is only supported by interpenetration metrics; no contact/support analysis (e.g., gravity stability, resting contact) is performed, so collision-awareness should not be conflated with physical plausibility.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined problem: compositional 3D generation that preserves object-object spatial relationships (OOR) and avoids interpenetration, which is valuable for robot simulation data curation.

Sensible training-free pipeline design: using image-guided 3D generation (scene reconstruction + PartField segmentation) as spatial guidance, then reformulating composition as global-to-local registration (GeoTransformer warm-start + scale-aware ICP) followed by an SDF-based collision penalty with an annealed schedule (Eq. 3). The components are well integrated and the method section is generally clear.

The VLM-driven agentic refinement loop addresses a genuine failure mode (geometrically incompatible complementary assets due to 2D occlusion) that pure pose optimization cannot fix; the qualitative examples (Figs. 4, 8) are convincing.

Substantial dataset contribution (~8,300 interactive pairs across 9 categories, including ~600 multi-object scenes) that is an order of magnitude larger than 2BY2's 517 pairs and will be publicly released; appropriate attribution of prior datasets.

Reasonably thorough evidence for an applied/systems contribution: quantitative comparison against three baseline families (Table 2), a careful ablation isolating the global-to-local scheme, the SDF term, and the agentic loop (Table 3), multi-part extension (Figs. 6, 11, 12), multi-view validation (Figs. 13-15), and an honest failure analysis (Fig. 9, Sec. A.4).
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on proprietary, closed-source services (Nano Banana Pro / Gemini for image editing and VLM analysis, commercial 3D platforms). This significantly threatens reproducibility: the pipeline's behavior may change with model updates, and reimplementing the system with open alternatives is non-trivial. The code/dataset availability statement is also incomplete in the manuscript (the URL appears truncated/missing).

Limited algorithmic novelty: the core contributions are an integration of known techniques (GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, SDF repulsion penalty, VLM agent loops). This is acceptable for an Applied/Systems contribution, but the paper does not deeply analyze when/why the design works (e.g., sensitivity to PartField segmentation quality, anchor-selection heuristic given only empirically).

Evaluation has weaknesses: 150 test cases generated by the authors' own pipeline; the human rating protocol (number of raters, blinding, expertise) is unspecified; VLM-based ratings may systematically favor outputs that resemble the generative models used in the pipeline; and the surface/volume intersection metrics are directly optimized by the SDF objective, so the improvement on those metrics is partly expected by construction. No statistical significance or variance is reported.

A directly relevant zero-shot baseline, COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE [8], which also uses VLM-guided text optimization for pairwise object composition, is discussed in related work but not compared against; feed-forward baselines (MIDI, Jigsaw, 2BY2) are evaluated out of their training distribution, which makes those comparisons somewhat unfair even if the qualitative conclusions are plausible.

Runtime/compute cost of the full pipeline (number of Nano Banana Pro calls, TRELLIS2 reconstructions, agentic iterations, wall-clock time per scene) is not reported, which matters for claims of 'scalable and automated synthesis'; failure rate on the additional 140 cases (29/140 reported) suggests roughly 20% failure, which deserves more discussion relative to the framing.

Dataset curation quality control, licensing of the underlying meshes, and how compositional poses were verified (automatic filtering vs. manual checking) are not described, limiting assessment of dataset reliability.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: generating compositional, interaction-ready 3D object pairs with correct object-object spatial relationships, motivated by the scarcity of interactive 3D data for robot simulation.

The generate-then-compose reframing of compositional generation as a guided registration problem is a sensible and practical design, and the two-stage pipeline (global-to-local anchoring followed by SDF-based collision-aware refinement) is clearly described and technically reasonable.
A well-designed ablation study (Table 3) isolates the contributions of each component (GeoTransformer initialization, SDF term, agentic loop), which strengthens the empirical case.
The paper is candid about failure modes (symmetric ambiguity, occlusion-induced collisions, mesh holes in Figures 7 and 9) and includes a meaningful limitations/future-work discussion.
The announced dataset of ~8,300 compositional 3D scenes across 9 categories is potentially a valuable community resource relative to prior pairwise-composition datasets (e.g., 2BY2's 517 pairs).
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed, proprietary models (Nano Banana Pro for image generation/editing and Gemini 3 Pro as the VLM) makes the pipeline effectively non-reproducible and its long-term availability uncertain. The claimed 'fully automated pipeline' is really a choreography of third-party black-box systems, and results may change silently as these models are updated.

The core contribution is an assembly of existing techniques (GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, OBB scale estimation, SDF penetration penalties, VLM-in-the-loop editing) rather than a new algorithmic insight. As a training-free systems paper this is acceptable, but the novelty bar is only marginally met, and the method's quality largely reflects the quality of TRELLIS2 and Nano Banana Pro rather than the composition machinery itself.

The claim of 'physically-sound' / 'physically plausible' compositions is overclaimed. The SDF term only penalizes interpenetration between two meshes; there is no physics-simulation validation (stability, contact, support, gravity) despite the paper's motivation being Sim2Real robot training. Object pairs resting in thin air or other non-physical contact configurations would not be caught by the metrics.

The evaluation protocol has self-favoring circularity: semantic fidelity is measured by CLIP against the very Nano Banana Pro-generated image that the method's outputs are derived from, and human/VLM ratings are reported as single averages with no protocol details (number of raters, criteria, variance, statistical significance). The 150-case test set is small and the baselines (Jigsaw, 2BY2, MIDI) are applied far outside their training distributions, making some comparisons unfair in the method's favor.

Several important details are missing: how the dataset's compositional poses are validated or quality-filtered; licensing of dataset assets generated from proprietary models; runtime/cost per scene (the agentic loop re-runs image editing and 3D generation up to 5 times); and no code or dataset is actually available yet, only a promise.

The framework's success is bottlenecked by the initial 2D guidance image: since the final composition explicitly mimics the spatial configuration of the TRELLIS2-generated scene, the method inherits all of its errors (as the authors concede in A.4), which limits the perceived benefit over simply post-processing the generated scene.

Minor issues: the method description in Section 4.4 and Figure 4 implies the VLM may regenerate geometry that no longer matches the user's intent, with no mechanism to verify semantic consistency of the corrected asset; some notation (M vs. M' roles) takes effort to track; and 'extensive experiments' amounts to one table plus mostly qualitative figures.

strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem: automated synthesis of collision-aware interactive 3D object pairs is relevant for Sim2Real/robot simulation, and the insight of using image-guided 3D generation (TRELLIS2 scene reconstructions) as spatial priors for a registration problem is a sensible and elegant reframing.

Training-free pipeline that composes existing components (Nano Banana Pro for 2D editing, TRELLIS2 for reconstruction, PartField for coarse spatial cues, GeoTransformer+scale-aware ICP for global-to-local registration, SDF penalty for collision avoidance) into a coherent, extensible framework; the two-stage anchor/remaining decomposition is clearly described.

Solid experimental evidence: quantitative comparison over 150 cases against three categories of baselines (feed-forward, direct segmentation, classical registration), an ablation study (Table 3) that isolates each component (global-to-local scheme, SDF term, agentic loop), multi-part extension demos, and a frank failure-case analysis (Figure 7, 9).

Additional dataset contribution (~8,300 interactive pairs across 9 categories, including 600 multi-object scenes) that is substantially larger than prior pairwise composition data (e.g., 2BY2's 517 pairs), potentially valuable for future research.
The VLM-based agentic refinement loop is a reasonable mechanism for semantic-level corrections that pose optimization alone cannot achieve, and is illustrated with concrete iterative examples.
Clear writing overall, with a notation table, well-defined problem setup, and explicit limitation discussion (symmetric-ambiguity inversions, 2D-occlusion-induced priors, fine-grained joints).
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source, proprietary components (Nano Banana Pro / Gemini 3 Pro, commercial APIs). This significantly limits reproducibility of the claimed fully-automated pipeline, and the manuscript provides no code link at submission time ('code and dataset will be available' is a promise, not evidence).

The technical novelty is moderate: the pipeline is primarily an engineering combination of known tools (GeoTransformer, scale-aware ICP, standard SDF penetration penalties, VLM prompt loops). The 'physically-sound' claim is arguably overstated—the method enforces collision avoidance via an SDF penalty, but performs no actual physical simulation or stability/contact reasoning; support relationships and frictional stability are not addressed.

Baseline fairness concerns: Jigsaw and 2BY2 were trained for different tasks/data distributions (fracture assembly, 2BY2's own data) and are evaluated far out of domain, which partly explains their poor scores; the strongest recent competitors for this setting (e.g., COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE, OmniPart/SAM3D for part-level generation) are discussed in related work but not compared empirically. The 'ours' pipeline also has access to the compositional 2D image and text prompt that some baselines lack.

Quantitative metrics have weaknesses: human/VLM ratings on 150 cases lack details on rater count, protocol, and variance; CLIP scores against the Nano-Banana-Pro-generated image partially measure consistency with the same generative prior the pipeline exploits. Test cases are drawn from figures/curated prompts, so selection bias is possible.

The agentic refinement loop is only qualitatively characterized; no statistics on convergence rate, iterations needed, failure-to-converge rate, or cost per refinement across the 8,300-scene dataset are given, making it hard to assess practical throughput despite the dataset-scale claims.
Dataset provenance and licensing are not discussed (assets are produced by generative models with unclear rights), and how pose annotations θ were validated for correctness/quality is not described.

The paper tail is somewhat loose: an unfinished URL in the abstract-adjacent text, several appendix statements are assertions without supporting statistics, and there is no societal-impact discussion of large-scale synthetic asset generation.
